plain_english: Start by deciding what kind of person you want to be. Choose a character and way of acting that you can stick to whether you're alone or with others.
original_excerpt: Begin by prescribing to yourself some character and demeanor, such as you may preserve both alone and in company.

plain_english: Stay quiet most of the time. When you do speak, say only what's necessary. Keep it brief. You can join conversations sometimes when it makes sense, but don't let them drag on about the usual stuff—gladiators, horse races, athletes, food, or drink. Those are shallow topics. And especially don't talk about people in ways that criticize them, praise them, or compare them to others. If you can steer the conversation toward better subjects, do it. But if you're stuck with strangers, just stay quiet.
original_excerpt: Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words. We may, however, enter sparingly into discourse sometimes, when occasion calls for it; but let it not run on any of the common subjects, as gladiators, or horse races, or athletic champions, or food, or drink—the vulgar topics of conversation—and especially not on men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons. If you are able, then, by your own conversation, bring over that of your company to proper subjects; but if you happen to find yourself among strangers, be silent.

plain_english: Don't laugh too loud, too often, or too much. Avoid making promises and oaths if you can. At least keep them to a minimum.
original_excerpt: Let not your laughter be loud, frequent, or abundant. Avoid taking oaths, if possible, altogether; at any rate, so far as you are able.

plain_english: Stay away from crude, lowbrow entertainment. But if you have to attend something like that, stay alert. Don't let yourself slip into bad behavior without noticing. Here's why: even if you're a good person, hanging around corrupt people will corrupt you too.
original_excerpt: Avoid public and vulgar entertainments; but if ever an occasion calls you to them, keep your attention upon the stretch, that you may not imperceptibly slide into vulgarity. For be assured that if a person be ever so pure himself, yet, if his companion be corrupted, he who converses with him will be corrupted likewise.

plain_english: Give your body only what it absolutely needs: food, drink, clothes, shelter, basic help. Cut out anything that's just for show or luxury.
original_excerpt: Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires, as meat, drink, clothing, house, retinue. But cut off everything that looks toward show and luxury.

plain_english: Before you get married, do everything you can to avoid sleeping with women you shouldn't sleep with. But don't be harsh or judgmental toward people who do this. And don't keep bragging that you're better than them.
original_excerpt: Before marriage guard yourself with all your ability from unlawful intercourse with women; yet be not uncharitable or severe to those who are led into this, nor boast frequently that you yourself do otherwise.

plain_english: If someone tells you that another person said bad things about you, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, respond: "He doesn't know about my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned just these."
original_excerpt: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: "He was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone."

plain_english: You don't need to go to public events very often. But when you do go, don't care more about anyone else than yourself. Just want things to happen as they happen, and want the best person to win. This way, nothing will disappoint you. Don't cheer, don't make fun of anyone, and don't get worked up. When you leave, don't spend a lot of time talking about what happened if it doesn't help you improve yourself. Talking too much about it shows you were too impressed by the spectacle.
original_excerpt: It is not necessary for you to appear often at public spectacles; but if ever there is a proper occasion for you to be there, do not appear more solicitous for any other than for yourself—that is, wish things to be only just as they are, and only the best man to win; for thus nothing will go against you. But abstain entirely from acclamations and derision and violent emotions. And when you come away, do not discourse a great deal on what has passed and what contributes nothing to your own amendment. For it would appear by such discourse that you were dazzled by the show.

plain_english: Don't be eager to attend private readings or performances. But if you do go, keep your composure and dignity. Just don't be a jerk about it.
original_excerpt: Be not prompt or ready to attend private recitations; but if you do attend, preserve your gravity and dignity, and yet avoid making yourself disagreeable.

plain_english: When you're about to meet with someone, especially someone who seems more important than you, ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would handle it. You'll know what to do when things come up.
original_excerpt: When you are going to confer with anyone, and especially with one who seems your superior, represent to yourself how Socrates or Zeno would behave in such a case, and you will not be at a loss to meet properly whatever may occur.

plain_english: When you're going to meet someone powerful, imagine the worst-case scenarios first. Maybe they won't be there. Maybe you'll be turned away. Maybe the doors will be locked. Maybe they'll ignore you completely. If you still have good reason to go, then go. Accept whatever happens. Don't tell yourself afterward, 'That wasn't worth the trouble.' That kind of thinking is cheap. It's what people do when they let outside things control them.
original_excerpt: When you are going before anyone in power, fancy to yourself that you may not find him at home, that you may be shut out, that the doors may not be opened to you, that he may not notice you. If, with all this, it be your duty to go, bear what happens and never say to yourself, "It was not worth so much"; for this is vulgar, and like a man bewildered by externals.

plain_english: When you're with other people, don't constantly talk about your own actions and dangers. You might enjoy talking about the risks you've taken, but other people don't enjoy hearing your stories as much as you think. Also avoid trying too hard to make people laugh. This can easily make you seem crude. Plus it might make people respect you less. Stay away from dirty talk too. When someone starts going down that path, speak up and shut it down if you can. If you can't, at least show you disapprove — stay quiet, look embarrassed, and give them a serious look.
original_excerpt: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers. For however agreeable it may be to yourself to allude to the risks you have run, it is not equally agreeable to others to hear your adventures. Avoid likewise an endeavor to excite laughter, for this may readily slide you into vulgarity, and, besides, may be apt to lower you in the esteem of your acquaintance. Approaches to indecent discourse are likewise dangerous. Therefore, when anything of this sort happens, use the first fit opportunity to rebuke him who makes advances that way, or, at least, by silence and blushing and a serious look show yourself to be displeased by such talk.
